samples.question: The picture shows three framed panels stacked one above the other. Each panel contains exactly one coloured trace, drawn as a line through nine round markers that run from left to right; one trace is red, one is green and one is blue. Every panel is ruled with the same horizontal gridlines and every panel uses the same spacing between neighbouring gridlines, so a vertical distance means the same thing in all three panels. For one trace, a FALL is measured between two of its own markers: pick any marker, then pick a marker further to the RIGHT along the same trace that sits lower, and the size of that fall is the vertical distance between them. A trace's DEEPEST FALL is the largest such distance it contains, that is, the biggest drop from an earlier high point down to a later low point. Order matters: a trace that starts low and climbs to a high point has only a small deepest fall no matter how much total height it covers, so the trace that spans the most gridlines from its lowest to its highest marker is often not the answer, and neither is the trace that reaches the lowest marker in its own panel. Compare each trace only with itself; a marker in one panel is never paired with a marker in another. In every picture each trace contains at least one fall, and no two traces have equally deep deepest falls. The colours and the top-to-bottom order of the panels carry no information. Which coloured trace has the deepest fall? Answer red, green or blue.
